sections.COMMENTS:
This Individual Source represents the fault activated on 24 August 2016, the first mainshock of the 2016-17 central Italy seismic sequence (e.g., Michele et al., 2016; Tinti et al., 2016; Chiaraluce et al., 2017; Cirella et al., 2018; Improta et al., 2019; Michele et al., 2020).
The 2016-17 sequence initiated during the summer of 2016 and includes a succession of moderate to strong extensional earthquakes. These events activated a ca. 70 km long, NNW-SSE trending, multiple fault systems, exhibiting complex ruptures along the backbone of the central Apennines. These events have notoriously and vastly affected the towns of Amatrice, Visso, and Norcia.
This Individual Source is part of a WSW-dipping normal fault system, formed during the Mesozoic and reactivated during the Miocene due to the flexure of the foreland in response of the orogenic building (Tondi et al., 2020). Later, during the development of the Acquasanta thrust sheet (Scisciani and Montefalcone, 2005), the Monti della Laga - Gorzano (MLG) fault system was transported onto the thrust hanging-wall.
The interpretation of seismic reflection profiles in the area (Porreca et al., 2018; Di Bucci et al., 2021, www.retrace3d.it) allowed to image a) the Acquasanta thrust geometry (Buttinelli et al., 2021), that dips toward W-NW, and b) the northern segment of MLG on its hanging-wall, that reaches seismogenic depths in the sector between the towns of Amatrice and Accumoli. To the north, while not mapped in the surface geology, MLG is overthrusted by the Olevano-Antrodoco-Sibillini (OAS) thrust near the Mt. Vettore. The sector of MLG north of Amatrice hosted the 24 August 2016 mainshock (Bonini et al., 2016; Valensise et al., 2016; Buttinelli et al., 2021).
Historical and instrumental catalogues (ISIDe Working Group, 2007; Guidoboni et al., 2019; Rovida et al., 2021) show a very dense intermediate (4.5 < Mw < 5.0) to damaging seismicity within the area. This region has been affected by the 7 October 1639 (Mw 6.2) and the 28 April 1646 (Mw 5.9) Monti della Laga earthquakes (Galli et al., 2016).
This Source results from the extensive studies performed in the area following the 2016-17 seismic sequence (e.g., Michele et al., 2016; Chiaraluce et al., 2017; Improta et al., 2019; Michele et al., 2020), focal mechanisms (e.g., Tinti et al., 2016; Scognamiglio et al., 2016), slip patch distribution (e.g., Tinti et al., 2016; Cirella et al., 2018), geodetic displacement from InSAR data (e.g., Cheloni et al., 2016; Huang et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2018), local ERT data (Villani et al., 2019), and the analysis of the 3D geological model built within the area (Di Bucci et al., 2021; www.retrace.it). Various investigators addressed the active tectonics and, subsequently, the seismogenic characteristics of the area, with widely divergent interpretations.
After the 24 August earthquake, ground ruptures were discontinuously identified along the MLG fault, whereas abundant ground ruptures were observed along the western flank of Mt. Vettore (EMERGEO Working Group, 2016, 2017; Civico et al., 2018; Villani et al., 2019). These were interpreted as primary coseismic ruptures (e.g., Pucci et al., 2017; Brozzetti et al., 2019) or due to shaking-induced mechanisms, such as gravity-driven displacement, compaction, and secondary ground failure (e.g., Aringoli et al., 2016; Huang et al., 2017; Di Naccio et al., 2019).
The geodetic and seismological data highlight the presence of two main patches of slip during the 24 August 2016 earthquake (Tinti et al., 2016; Cheloni et al., 2017; Cirella et al., 2018), suggesting a complex rupture with a relatively high-angle dip in the southern sector (45Â°-50Â°) and a relatively low-angle dip in the northern sector (30Â°-40Â°), possibly involving the reactivation of inherited thrusts (Bonini et al., 2016) or a double fault system including the northern part of MLG fault and the Redentore-Vettoretto fault merging together at depth (Lavecchia et al., 2016).
Alternatively, Pizzi et al., (2017) propose that OAS splits the growing normal fault system (MLG to the south and Monte Vettore - Monte Bove to the north) and acted as a barrier for the 24 August 2016.
The reader should notice that this Individual Source is modeled as a single rectilinear rupture, as for any Individual Source anywhere else in the Database, despite the fact that the 24 August 2016 rupture exhibits a complex geometry made up of two slip patches (e.g., Tinti et al., 2016; Cirella et al., 2018), respectively to the south and to the north of the OAS (Bonini et al., 2016).

pictures.t: Focal mechanism solutions of the first month of the 2016-2017 Central Italy sequence
pictures.c: Time Domain Moment Tensor (TDMT) solutions of the first month (August 24th- September 25th) of the 2016-2017 Central Italy seismic sequence. Most of the focal mechanisms show NNWâ€“SSE striking normal faults in agreement with the main NE-SW extensional deformation of Central Apennines (Scognamiglio et al., [2016])

pictures.t: Rupture model of the 24 August 2016 earthquake by inverting ground velocity time histories
pictures.c: Rupture model of the 24 August 2016 earthquake by inverting waveforms from 26 three-component strong motion accelerometers. Notice that the slip distribution is heterogeneous and characterized by two slip patches (Tinti et al., [2016])

pictures.t: Surface projection of the inverted slip distribution of the 24 August 2016 earthquake
pictures.c: Surface projection of (a) the inverted slip distribution of the 24 August 2016 earthquake (color scale, expressed in meters) and (b) the early aftershocks (gray dots) (Tinti et al., [2016])

pictures.t: Inverted rupture model of the 24 August 2016 Amatrice earthquake
pictures.c: Detailed description of the rupture propagation of the 24 August 2016 Amatrice earthquake: (a) slip, (b) rise time, (c) velocity amplitudes, (d) rupture index, (e) time snapshots of slip velocity. The source model reveals a high degree of complexity, characterized by a bilateral rupture and two well-separated slip patches (Cirella et al., [2018])

pictures.t: Evidence of coseismically triggered landslides near Monte Vettore and Castelluccio - map view
pictures.c: Landslides triggered by the 24 August 2016 earthquake ground shaking in areas of Mt. Vettore and Castelluccio from inversion of coseismic GPS and InSAR data. Notice that the landslide near Mt. Vettore terminates on the preexisting Monte Vettore Fault scarp (Huang et al., [2017])

pictures.t: Evidence of coseismically triggered landslides near Monte Vettore and Castelluccio - cross sections
pictures.c: Cross sections of GPS-InSAR and topographic data showing the triggered landslides by the 24 August 2016 earthquake. The deformation along the west facing side of the Mt. Vettore extend no more than 5 km and is consistent with field survey after the earthquake (Huang et al., [2017])

pictures.t: Slip distribution of the two-fault geometry of the 24 August 2016 earthquake
pictures.c: Inferred fault geometry and slip distribution of the two-fault system responsible for the 24 August 2016 earthquake. Notice that the main asperities are located at two different segments: a steeper (dip 53Â°) southern fault segment than the northern segment (dip 43Â°) (Huang et al., [2017])

pictures.t: Field coseismic effects of the 24 August 2016 earthquake in an area of about 750 km2
pictures.c: Field surveying of more than 3200 coseismic effects (ruptures, fractures, and landslides) collected by the Emergeo Working Group before the occurrence of the seismic events of October. Notice that the most continuous coseismic evidence was found along the western side of the Mt. Vettore (Emergeo Working Group [2016])

pictures.t: Field geological effects of the 24 August 2016 earthquake in the Mt. Vettore area
pictures.c: Surface ruptures with vertical / horizontal offset observed along the western side of the Mt. Vettore for about 5 km, only a number of investigators intrerpreted these brittle features as effects of primary surface faulting (Emergeo Working Group [2016])

pictures.t: Simplified causative faults of the 24 August 2016 earthquake
pictures.c: Sketch showing the simplified causative faults of the 24 August 2016 earthquake. Three faults played a role: F#1: SSW-dipping normal fault, F#2: portion of the Sibillini Thrust reactivated in an extensional fashion; F#3: antithetic normal fault. Notice that this reconstruction was published a few weeks after the 24 August earthquake and was the first to suggest the active role of the thrust (Bonini et al., [2016])

pictures.t: Inversion of DInSAR data
pictures.c: Inversion of Synthetic Aperture Radar Interferometry (DInSAR) data from ALOS-2 and CSK satellites (Cirella et al., [2018])

pictures.t: Comparison among InSAR models and dislocation models
pictures.c: InSAR models from normal faulting earthquakes: (a) 1997 Colfiorito, (b) 2009 L'Aquila, (c) 24 August 2016, (d) 1995 Dinar (Turkey) and conceptual dislacement models (Valensise et al. [2016])

pictures.t: Central Apennines seismicity after 2016-17 seismic sequence
pictures.c: Relocated events of the 2016-17 seismic sequence in Central Apennines (Michele et al., [2020])

pictures.t: Seismological geological and geodetic observations for the 30 October 2016 Mw 6.5 earthquake
pictures.c: (a) Early aftershocks of the 2016 seismic sequence (b) Displacement field from InSAR S1-A data (c) Coseismic GPS diplacement (d) coseismic features after the 24 August and 30 October 2016 mainshock (Bonini et al., [2019])

pictures.t: Geogical map of the area affected by the 2016-17 Seismic sequence
pictures.c: Geological scheme and stratigraphic units of the Central Apennines (Buttinelli et al., [2021])

pictures.t: Seismic reflection profile across the Sibillini and Acquasanta thrusts
pictures.c: Uninterpreted and interpreted seismic reflection profile across the Sibillini and Acquasanta thrust (Buttinelli et al., [2021])

pictures.t: Geological cross sections in the Central Apennines and projected seismicity
pictures.c: Geological cross sections across the Central Apennine area affected by the 2016-17 seismic sequence extracted from a 3D geological model (RETRACE-3D, http://www.retrace3d.it/) showing also the seismicity within 1 km from the section traces (from Buttinelli et al., [2021])

pictures.t: Olevano-Antrodoco-Sibillini Line, seismogenic sources, and geofluids
pictures.c: Relationships between tectonics and geofluids in the inner Apennines. An alignment of thermal springs and CO2 emissions highlights the presence of the Olevano-Antrodoco-Sibillini Line (OASL), a major tectonic lineament, that plays a role in controlling the segmentation of seismogenic faults in central Italy (Vannoli et al., [2021]).

pictures.t: Geological, seismological, and geodetic data of the 2016-2017 seismic sequence
pictures.c: (a) Semplified geological map, (b) main slip patches of 24 August and 26 October 2016 earthquakes, and (c) coseismic deformation of the 26 October and 30 October 2016 earthquakes (Scognamiglio et al., [2018])

pictures.t: Comparison between the slip distributions of the 24 August and the 30 October 2016 earthquakes
pictures.c: Comparison between the slip distributions of the 24 August Amatrice (in red) and the 30 October Norcia (in blue) 2016 main shocks. A slip patch located between the two asperities that ruptured during the 24 August event, just below Accumoli and Arquata del Tronto, demonstrate continuity in the coseismic rupture propagation along and on the single fault plane that ruptured during the first main shock of the sequence (Scognamiglio et al., [2018])

pictures.t: Deep-seated gravitational slope deformation (DSGSD) in the Mt. Vettore area
pictures.c: Deep-seated gravitational slope deformation (DSGSD) along the western slope of Mt. Vettore triggered by the 24 August 2016 earthquake  (Aringoli et al., [2016])

pictures.t: Central Apennines seismotectonic map
pictures.c: Map showing the 2009 earthquake epicentral area in the seismotectonic framework of the Central Apennines (from Falcucci et al. [2009]).
